title: Taking Part in Your Community
tagline: Speak up, bring evidence, and help decisions get made.
description: Communities change when people take part: in ward meetings, consultations, community groups and peaceful action. This course shows you where local decisions are made, how to raise an issue with evidence, how to work with others, and how to make sure everyone, including women, youth and people with disabilities, has a voice.
outcomes: Name where local decisions are made
Take part in ward meetings and public consultations
Raise an issue clearly with evidence
Report a community problem and follow it up
Organise peacefully, including petitions and meetings
Run a fair, inclusive community group

lessons.title: Where decisions are made
lessons.body:
Many decisions that affect your daily life are made **close to home**, not only in Lusaka.

## Local decision-makers
- **Your council** decides on markets, local roads, refuse, planning and building permits, and local by-laws. Councillors vote on these in **council meetings**.
- **Ward Development Committees (WDCs)** identify local needs and propose and monitor projects in each ward.
- **CDF committees** decide which community projects and applications get Constituency Development Fund money.
- **School boards** and **parent-teacher associations** influence how schools are run.
- **Health centre committees** link communities with clinics.
- **Traditional leaders** make many decisions on customary land and community matters in chiefdoms.

## National decision-makers
- **Parliament** passes laws and the budget.
- **Ministries** make policies and plans, often after **consultation**.

## Why local matters
It is often easier to influence a decision in your ward or district than in Lusaka. Councillors and committee members live nearby, and local projects are visible: you can see whether the borehole works.

## Find out who is who
Make a short list:
- your ward name and councillor,
- your constituency and MP,
- members of your WDC,
- the council's main office and its phone number.

Keep it on your phone. When an issue comes up, you will know exactly who to contact.
key_points: Many decisions are made locally
WDCs and CDF committees decide local projects
Know your councillor, MP and WDC members
lessons.try_it: Write down your ward, councillor, constituency and MP.

lessons.title: Ward meetings and council meetings
lessons.body:
Meetings are where community voices turn into decisions.

## Ward meetings
Ward Development Committees and councillors hold **ward meetings** to discuss local needs and projects, including CDF proposals. These are your chance to:

- raise problems in your area,
- suggest projects, such as a borehole, a footbridge or a classroom,
- hear updates on projects already running.

Ask your councillor when and where the next meeting is. Notices may be put up at schools, churches, markets or the council office.

## Council meetings
Full council meetings are where councillors debate and decide. They are generally **open to the public** to observe. Agendas and minutes may be available from the council. Ask the council secretary or town clerk's office.

## Preparing to speak
- Arrive on time and sign the attendance register.
- Write your point in **one or two sentences**.
- Bring **facts**: dates, numbers, photos.
- Suggest a **solution** if you can.
- Speak politely and briefly. Let others speak too.

## After the meeting
- Note what was decided and **who** will act, and **by when**.
- Ask for a copy of the **minutes**.
- Follow up at the next meeting: *"Last month we agreed the drainage would be cleared. What has happened?"*

## Bring others
Ten residents raising the same issue carry more weight than one. Invite neighbours, especially those most affected.
key_points: Ward meetings are where local needs are raised
Council meetings are generally open to observe
Prepare one clear point with facts and a solution
lessons.try_it: Ask your councillor when the next ward meeting is.

lessons.title: Public consultations and submissions
lessons.body:
Before making big decisions, government often asks the public for views. These are called **consultations**.

## Examples
- **Pre-budget consultations** by the Ministry of Finance and National Planning.
- Consultations on new **laws and policies**.
- **Council planning** consultations, such as for a new market or land use plan.
- **Parliamentary committees** inviting **submissions** on Bills and issues.
- **Environmental assessments** for big projects such as mines, dams and roads, where affected communities should be consulted.

## Finding them
Watch for notices in **newspapers**, on **radio**, on the **official pages** of ministries and the National Assembly, and on council notice boards. Civil society organisations often share them too.

## Making a submission
A **submission** is a short written statement of your views.

1. Say **who you are**: a resident, a group, a farmers' cooperative.
2. Say **what** you are responding to.
3. Give your **main points**, numbered, each with a reason or example.
4. Make **recommendations**: what should change.
5. Keep it short, clear and polite.

Groups can make submissions together. It is often more powerful when many people agree.

## Speaking at a consultation meeting
If there is a public hearing or meeting, prepare like for a ward meeting: one clear point, facts, and a suggestion.

## Follow up
Ask how views will be used, and look for the final decision or report. Your submission becomes part of the public record.
key_points: Consultations ask the public for views before decisions
A submission is a short, clear written statement
Groups can submit together for more weight
lessons.try_it: Look for one current public consultation on a ministry's or Parliament's official page.

modules.title: Speaking up
modules.summary: Evidence, reporting problems and peaceful action.

lessons.title: Speak up with evidence
lessons.body:
A complaint backed by evidence is hard to ignore. A complaint based on rumours is easy to dismiss.

## What counts as evidence
- **Photos and videos** you took yourself, with dates.
- **Numbers**: how many households, how many days, how far people walk.
- **Documents**: letters, receipts, project boards, budgets, minutes.
- **Statements** from people affected, with their permission.
- Information received through an **access to information request**.

## Collect it carefully
- Visit the site yourself.
- Take clear photos from several angles.
- Write down what you see, with the date and place.
- Ask affected people simple questions and note their answers.

## Present it simply
Turn your evidence into a short message:

*"The footbridge at Mutanda stream collapsed on 2 February. 150 pupils from Kalimba now walk an extra 4 km to school. During the rains, some miss school completely. We ask the council to repair the bridge before the next rainy season."*

Facts, impact, and a clear request.

## Be honest
- Separate what you **know** from what you **think**.
- Do not exaggerate numbers.
- Do not accuse named people of wrongdoing without proof.

Honest evidence builds trust. Exaggeration destroys it.

## Protect people
Ask permission before photographing or quoting people. Do not share private information, especially of children.
key_points: Evidence includes photos, numbers and documents
Facts, impact and a clear request
Never exaggerate or accuse without proof
lessons.try_it: Write a three-sentence message about a local issue: facts, impact, request.

lessons.title: Practice: reporting a community problem
lessons.body:
*The drainage along the main road in your compound is blocked. Every time it rains, water floods into homes and the market. It has happened three times this season.*

## Step 1: Gather facts
- Take photos of the blocked drain and the flooding, with dates.
- Count roughly how many homes and stalls are affected.
- Ask neighbours when it started and whether anyone has reported it.

## Step 2: Report to the right office
Drainage is usually a **council** responsibility. Report it to the council's engineering or public health office, by visit, letter or official phone line. Ask for a **reference number**.

## Step 3: Tell your councillor
Send your councillor a short message with the photos and reference. Ask them to follow up and to raise it at the next **ward meeting**.

## Step 4: Organise neighbours
Ask affected neighbours to sign a short **letter** supporting the request. Include their names, plot numbers and signatures. Many voices add weight.

## Step 5: Follow up
After two weeks, follow up with your reference. Keep a record of each contact.

## Step 6: Think about what you can do together
While waiting, can the community organise a **clean-up** of rubbish blocking the drain, safely and with the council's knowledge? Communities and councils working together often get faster results.

## Step 7: Share progress
Tell neighbours what happened. If it is fixed, thank the council publicly. That encourages good service.
key_points: Facts and photos first
Report to the council and get a reference
Organise neighbours and follow up
lessons.try_it: Choose one problem in your area and plan the first three steps.

lessons.title: Petitions and peaceful action
lessons.body:
When meetings and complaints are not enough, communities can take **peaceful collective action**. The Constitution protects freedom of assembly and expression, with limits to protect public safety and others' rights.

## Petitions
A **petition** is a letter signed by many people asking for a specific action.

- Address it to the right decision-maker: the council, a ministry, or Parliament.
- State the problem, the evidence and the request clearly.
- Collect names, NRC numbers or phone numbers, and signatures, only with people's agreement.
- Deliver it in person and get a **stamped copy**.

Citizens can also petition **Parliament** on issues of public concern. Ask your MP or the National Assembly office about the process.

## Public meetings and processions
For public gatherings and processions, the **Public Order Act** requires organisers to **notify the police in advance**. Organisers must also keep the event peaceful. Ask at your local police station about the current requirements and timelines.

## Using the media
- **Community radio** call-in programmes are widely heard.
- Local journalists may cover well-documented community problems.
- Social media can spread your message. Keep it factual and respectful.

## Peaceful always
Violence, damaging property and blocking roads hurt your own community, put people in danger, and can lead to arrests. They also make it easier to ignore your message. Peaceful, persistent and well-organised action is far more effective.

## Know when to get support
Civil society organisations, paralegals and community leaders can advise you on organising safely and lawfully.
key_points: A petition is a signed request for a specific action
Notify the police in advance of public gatherings
Peaceful, persistent action works best
lessons.try_it: Draft the one-sentence request a petition about a local issue would make.

modules.title: Working together
modules.summary: Community groups, inclusion and keeping momentum.

lessons.title: Community groups that make a difference
lessons.body:
Many changes happen through **groups**, not individuals. Zambia has a strong tradition of people working together.

## Types of groups
- **Savings groups** and **cooperatives**: members save, lend and invest together.
- **Parent-teacher associations (PTAs)**: improve schools and children's learning.
- **Neighbourhood watch** groups: improve safety, working with the police.
- **Youth and women's clubs**: build skills, start businesses and speak up.
- **Farmers' groups**: share knowledge, buy inputs and sell together.
- **Health and water committees**: look after boreholes and link with clinics.
- **Church and faith groups**: often lead community support.

## Starting a group
1. Bring together people who share a goal.
2. Agree the **purpose** in one sentence.
3. Choose **leaders** fairly, by election.
4. Agree simple **rules**: meetings, contributions, decisions.
5. Keep **records**: members, money, minutes.

## Registering
Some groups benefit from registering, for example to open a bank account or apply for CDF empowerment grants or loans. Clubs and cooperatives can register with the relevant authorities. Ask your district **Community Development** office or the council's CDF office for guidance on which registration suits your group.

## Working with others
Link your group with your **Ward Development Committee**, councillor, and local civil society organisations. Groups that work together often achieve much more.
key_points: Groups achieve more than individuals
Agree purpose, fair leadership, rules and records
Registration can help groups access funds
lessons.try_it: Think of one group in your community you could join or start.

lessons.title: Making sure everyone has a voice
lessons.body:
A community decision is better when **everyone** affected has a say. Some people are often left out, even when no one means to exclude them.

## Who is often left out
- **Women**, especially in public meetings.
- **Young people.**
- **People with disabilities.**
- **Elderly people.**
- People who **cannot read**, or who speak a different language.
- People who live far from the meeting place.

## Simple ways to include everyone
- Hold meetings at **times and places** people can reach, considering work, farming, markets and childcare.
- Choose places that are **accessible** for people using wheelchairs or crutches.
- Use the **local language**, and explain documents aloud.
- Invite women and youth to **speak**, and give space for their views. Some groups hold separate sessions so people feel comfortable.
- Share information through **many channels**: announcements at church, the market, radio, WhatsApp and word of mouth.
- Ask people directly: *"What do you think?"*

## In leadership
Encourage women, youth and people with disabilities to stand for leadership roles in committees and groups. Diverse leaders understand more of the community's needs.

## In projects
When planning a project, ask: *Who will benefit? Who might be harmed or left out?* For example, a new borehole should be reachable by elderly people and safe for women and children to use.

## Respect
Including everyone is not a favour. It is about the equal rights and dignity of every member of the community.
key_points: Plan meetings people can actually attend
Invite women, youth and people with disabilities to speak and lead
Ask who benefits and who is left out
lessons.try_it: At your next meeting, invite someone who usually stays quiet to share their view.

lessons.title: Keeping momentum and accountability
lessons.body:
Starting is exciting. Keeping going is harder. Good habits help groups and campaigns last.

## Meet regularly
Agree a regular time, such as the first Saturday of the month. Keep meetings short, with an **agenda**.

## Keep records
- **Minutes**: what was discussed, decided, who will act, and by when.
- **Money**: every contribution and expense, with receipts. Share the accounts with members regularly.
- **Contacts**: officials, partners and members.

## Share the work
Do not let one person do everything. Give each member a task. When people have a role, they stay involved.

## Be accountable
Leaders should report to members. Members should be able to ask questions about money and decisions without fear. Regular, fair **elections** for leaders keep groups healthy.

## Celebrate wins
When a borehole is fixed or a bridge repaired, celebrate and thank everyone who helped, including officials. It builds energy for the next goal.

## Learn from setbacks
Not everything works. Ask: what went well, what did not, and what will we do differently?

## Stay peaceful and non-partisan
Community work is for everyone. Keep groups open to people of all political views, tribes and religions. This makes your group stronger and harder to dismiss.

## Pass it on
Train new members, especially young people, so the work continues when current leaders step back.
key_points: Regular meetings, minutes and clear money records
Share tasks and hold fair elections
Celebrate wins and stay open to everyone
lessons.try_it: Write a simple agenda for a 30-minute community group meeting.
